Title: How Third‐Party Sellers Respond to Platform Owner Entry: Reselling Versus Private‐Label Modes in E‐Commerce
Authors: Shiying Zheng, Xiaodie Pu, Alain Yee Loong Chong
Affiliations: Nottingham University Business School China The University of Nottingham Ningbo China Ningbo China
Abstract: ABSTRACT E‐commerce platforms depend on a large base of third‐party sellers, yet platform owners increasingly enter the product markets of those sellers, competing with them while retaining control over the search rankings and recommendation systems that shape which products buyers encounter. Prior research on this phenomenon has produced mixed findings and has largely focused on innovation platforms (e.g., app stores and software ecosystems), leaving e‐commerce marketplaces comparatively underexplored. This study examines how third‐party sellers respond to two distinct modes of platform owner entry—reselling, in which the owner begins selling an existing product on the same product listing, and private‐label entry, in which the owner introduces a separately listed substitute whose exposure is also shaped by platform‐controlled search and recommendations. Using longitudinal data from Amazon.com and discontinuous growth modelling, we find that sellers immediately reduce prices following reselling entry but increase prices following private‐label entry. Over the longer term, both entry modes attenuate the trajectories of seller participation and investment in FBA relative to their pre‐entry trajectories, with stronger attenuation following private‐label entry. These findings extend research on platform owner entry by showing that third‐party seller responses vary systematically across entry modes, moving beyond treatments of owner entry as a single competitive event. They also develop a visibility‐based explanation for why seller responses differ across entry modes and show that pricing, participation and platform‐specific investment may unfold over different time horizons following platform owner entry.

Title: The importance of school quality ratings for school choices: Evidence from a nationwide system
Authors: Ellen Greaves, Iftikhar Hussain

Title: The Content Moderator’s Dilemma: Removal of Toxic Content and Distortions to Online Discourse
Authors: Mahyar Habibi, Carlo Schwarz, Carlo Schwarz
Affiliations: Bocconi University Department of Economics, , Milano, 20136; Bocconi University Department of Computing Sciences, , 20136
Abstract: Abstract There is an ongoing debate about how to moderate toxic speech on social media and the impact of content moderation on online discourse. This paper proposes and validates a methodology for measuring the content-moderation-induced distortions in online discourse using text embeddings from computational linguistics. Applying the method to a representative sample of 5 million US political Tweets, we find that removing toxic Tweets significantly alters the semantic composition of content. The magnitudes of the distortions are comparable to removing 4 out of 67 topics from the online discourse at random. This finding is consistent across different embedding models, toxicity metrics, and samples. Importantly, we demonstrate that these effects are not solely driven by toxic language but by the removal of topics often expressed in toxic form. We propose an alternative approach to content moderation that uses generative Large Language Models to rephrase toxic Tweets, preserving their salvageable content rather than removing them entirely. We show that this rephrasing strategy reduces toxicity while mitigating distortions in online content.

Title: Threat and Assimilation: Evidence from Refugees in Germany
Authors: Philipp Jaschke, Sulin Sardoschau, Marco Tabellini
Affiliations: Institute for Employment Research (IAB); Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin , RFBerlin, and IZA; Harvard Business School , NBER, CEPR, CReAM, and IZA
Abstract: Abstract This paper studies how local threat shapes refugees’ cultural assimilation and economic integration, exploiting plausibly exogenous variation in their allocation across German regions between 2013 and 2016. Using representative survey data and administrative records, we measure cultural preferences alongside employment, earnings, and job characteristics, and build a threat index combining contemporaneous and historical local xenophobia. Refugees assigned to more hostile regions converge more rapidly to Germans’ stated preferences, yet do not find jobs faster and experience slower earnings growth. We show that local hostility heightens threat perceptions, prompting quicker cultural adoption, while higher discrimination slows refugees’ successful economic integration.

Title: Knowledge diffusion, rising inequality, and the dynamics of a pulled front
Authors: Mark Staley
Affiliations: King’s Hill Research , 120 Adelaide Street West, Suite 2500, Toronto, Ontario M5H 1T1
Abstract: Abstract A model of economic growth is presented in which workers increase their labour income by learning from higher-paid workers. They also experience individual random income shocks. A calibration of the model to U.S. wage micro data implies that these shocks are Brownian ‘noise’, with drift close to zero. Growth comes from occasional random advances at the frontier, which create novel learning opportunities for others and drive sustained growth. The long-run growth rate is increasing in both the variance of shocks and the knowledge-diffusion rate. The model closely reproduces the evolving shape of the U.S. wage distribution between 1991 and 2023.

Title: Managing Procurement Auction Failure: Bid Requirements or Reserve Prices?
Authors: Jun Ma, Vadim Marmer, Pai Xu
Affiliations: School of Economics Renmin University of China Beijing China; Vancouver School of Economics University of British Columbia Vancouver Canada; Business School University of Hong Kong Hong Kong China
Abstract: ABSTRACT This paper examines bid requirements, where the government may cancel a procurement contract unless two or more bids are received. Using a first‐price auction model with endogenous entry, we compare the bid requirement and reserve price mechanisms in terms of auction failure and procurement costs. We find that, in comparison with bid requirements, reserve prices can reduce procurement costs and substantially lower failure probabilities, especially when entry costs are high or signals are sufficiently informative. Bid requirements are more likely to result in zero entry, while reserve prices can sustain positive entry under broader conditions.

Title: What Explains Growing Gender and Racial Education Gaps?
Authors: Zvi Eckstein, Michael Keane, Osnat Lifshitz
Affiliations: Reichman University Herzliya Israel; Johns Hopkins University Baltimore Maryland USA; University of New South Wales Sydney Australia
Abstract: ABSTRACT We study why US college graduation gaps by gender and race widened across cohorts. We develop a dynamic life‐cycle model with endogenous education, labor supply, marriage, fertility, and welfare participation. Preferences are fixed across cohorts and race/ethnic groups; changes arise from family background, labor‐market opportunities, and marriage markets. Labor‐market changes account for half of growth in women's graduation from the 1960 to 1980 cohorts. Parental background accounts for one quarter and marriage markets for one fifth. These shares are similar for Whites, Blacks, and Hispanics, but absolute gains were larger for White women, which led to wider racial gaps.

Title: Posterior inference of attitude-behaviour relationships using latent class choice models
Authors: Akshay Vij, Stephane Hess

Title: Regulation by Reputation? Intermediaries, Labor Abuses, and International Migration
Authors: A. Nilesh Fernando, Niharika Singh
Affiliations: King's College London; London School of Economics
Abstract: Abstract Migrant workers and employers rely on intermediaries to facilitate labor market placements. If information frictions obscure their reputation, however, intermediaries may underinvest in placement quality. Using data on more than 1.5 million Sri Lankan migrants to the Gulf region, we examine the effects of a government-run intermediary rating program that publicly revealed ratings two years after it was announced. Prior to the ratings’ public release, underperforming intermediaries invest in the rating criteria and place migrants in less abusive and more remunerative employment. Our results suggest the government’s threat of quality revelation induced intermediaries to prospectively screen employers and improve placement quality.
Journal: The Review of Economics and Statistics

Title: A Comment on “Raising Health Awareness in Rural Communities: A Randomized Experiment in Bangladesh and India” by Siddique et al. (2024)
Authors: Anders Kjelsrud, Andreas Kotsadam, Ole Rogeberg, Abel Brodeur
Affiliations: Oslo Metropolitan University; Ragnar Frisch Centre for Economic Research; University of Ottawa and Institute for Replication
Abstract: Abstract Siddique et al. (2024) report large effects of a mobile phone-based health awareness campaign in a field experiment conducted in rural Bangladesh and India during the COVID-19 pandemic. Treatments are stated as being randomized at the village level in the Bangladesh arm, but analyses of available replication materials from this and related field experiments show that this was not the case: participants retained their treatment group assignment from two earlier studies run by the same NGO. Because these earlier studies reported large and persistent treatment effects, the treatment groups in Siddique et al. (2024) could plausibly differ systematically, raising issues of confounding and interaction effects that invalidate the analyses and interpretations of this study, affecting both internal and external validity.
Journal: The Review of Economics and Statistics

Title: Response to the Comment on “Raising Health Awareness in Rural Communities: A Randomized Experiment in Bangladesh and India” (Siddique et al., 2024)
Authors: Firoz Ahmed, Asad Islam, Debayan Pakrashi
Journal: The Review of Economics and Statistics

Title: Author Requests for Removal from “Raising Health Awareness in Rural Communities: A Randomized Experiment in Bangladesh and India” (Siddique et al., 2024)
Authors: Abu Siddique, Tabassum Rahman
Affiliations: Associate Professor of Economics, Department of Economics, Royal Holloway University of London; Senior Research Fellow, Indigenous Epidemiology and Health Unit, Faculty of Medicine, Dentistry and Health Sciences, The University of Melbourne
Journal: The Review of Economics and Statistics

Title: The Unobserved Returns to Entrepreneurship
Authors: Sarada
Affiliations: University of California, Los Angeles
Abstract: Abstract This paper presents an alternative perspective to a long-standing empirical puzzle: that most entrepreneurs persevere despite persistently low earnings. Because entrepreneurial earnings are notoriously difficult to measure, I approach the question from an expenditure angle. I look at how switching into self-employment corresponds to changes in reported earnings versus expenditure. Using 45 years of longitudinal data, I find that individuals report earning 27.7% less in self-employment, while spending 3.8% more. This household expenditure premium accrues with entrepreneurial experience and is not offset by lower savings or longer work hours. The results hold in highly educated and incorporated business owner subsamples.
Journal: The Review of Economics and Statistics

Title: Misspecified Exponential Regressions: Estimation, Interpretation, and Average Marginal Effects
Authors: J. M. C. Santos Silva, Rainer Winkelmann
Affiliations: University of Surrey; University of Zurich
Abstract: Abstract Exponential regressions are frequently used when outcomes are non-negative. They are attractive because they are easy to interpret and to estimate, using pseudomaximum likelihood (PML). However, the validity of these methods depends on the correct specification of the conditional expectation, and little is known regarding their properties when the conditional expectation is misspecified. We show that PML estimators of misspecified exponential models provide optimal approximations to the conditional expectation, in a weighted mean squared error sense, and we give conditions under which their Poisson PML estimator identifies average marginal effects.
Journal: The Review of Economics and Statistics

Title: When Nurses Travel: Labor Supply Responses to Peak Demand for Nurses
Authors: Joshua D. Gottlieb, Avi Zenilman
Affiliations: University of Chicago and NBER; Corner Three Partners
Abstract: Abstract We study how a market uses temporary workers to accommodate extraordinary demand shocks. When COVID-19 surges, hospitals need additional nurses—especially in specialties central to COVID-19 care. By comparing markets for COVID-relevant and other specialties, we show that the market for travel nurses expands dramatically, and we estimate travel nurse labor supply across space. Supply is quite elastic, as workers can choose to travel where they are needed. Workers travel longer distances to temporary jobs when payment increases, suggesting that an integrated national market facilitates reallocation when demand spikes. But when national cases peak, travel distance is less responsive to local demand.
Journal: The Review of Economics and Statistics

Title: Estimating Nursing Home Quality with Selection
Authors: Andrew Olenski, Szymon Sacher
Affiliations: Yale School of Public Health and National Bureau of Economic Research; Stanford University
Abstract: Abstract We use variational inference (VI), a technique from the machine learning literature, to estimate a mortality-based Bayesian model of nursing home quality accounting for selection. We demonstrate how one can use VI to quickly and flexibly estimate a high-dimensional economic model with large datasets. Using our facility quality estimates, we examine the correlates of quality and find that public report cards have near-zero correlation. We then show that in contrast to prior literature, higher-quality nursing homes fared better during the pandemic: a one standard deviation increase in quality corresponds to 2.5% fewer COVID-19 cases.
Journal: The Review of Economics and Statistics

Title: Raising State Minimum Wages, Lowering Community College Enrollment
Authors: Diane Whitmore Schanzenbach, Julia A. Turner, Sarah Turner
Affiliations: Georgetown University and NBER; Northwestern University; University of Virginia and NBER
Abstract: Abstract Changes in the minimum wage may impact college enrollment and educational attainment. Using institutional data on college enrollment and program completion, we find that enrollment falls markedly among students at public two-year institutions in response to increases in the minimum wage. The largest enrollment effects are seen for those students who are enrolled part-time at community colleges. We find little evidence of negative effects on the attainment of certificates or degrees, suggesting that increases in the minimum wage are unlikely to divert students from degree attainment.
Journal: The Review of Economics and Statistics

Title: Asymptotics of Cointegration Tests for High-Dimensional Var(k)
Authors: Anna Bykhovskaya, Vadim Gorin
Affiliations: Duke University; University of California at Berkeley
Abstract: Abstract The paper studies nonstationary high-dimensional vector autoregressions of order k, VAR(k). Additional deterministic terms such as trend or seasonality are allowed. The number of time periods, T, and the number of coordinates, N, are assumed to be large and of the same order. Under this regime the first-order asymptotics of the Johansen likelihood ratio (LR), Pillai-Bartlett, and Hotelling-Lawley tests for cointegration are derived: The test statistics converge to nonrandom integrals. For more refined analysis, the paper proposes and analyzes a modification of the Johansen test. The new test for the absence of cointegration converges to the partial sum of the Airy1 point process. Supporting Monte Carlo simulations indicate that the same behavior persists universally in many situations beyond those considered in our theorems. The paper presents empirical implementations of the approach for the analysis of S&P100 stocks and of cryptocurrencies. The latter example has a strong presence of multiple cointegrating relationships, while the results for the former are consistent with the null of no cointegration.
Journal: The Review of Economics and Statistics

Title: Imposing Policy on Reluctant Actors: The Hospital Desegregation Campaign and Black Postneonatal Mortality in the Deep South
Authors: D. Mark Anderson, Kerwin Kofi Charles, Daniel I. Rees
Affiliations: Montana State University, IZA, and NBER; Yale University and NBER; Universidad Carlos III de Madrid
Abstract: Abstract In 1966, Southern hospitals were barred from participating in Medicare unless they discontinued their longstanding practice of racial segregation. Using data from five Deep South states and exploiting county-level variation in Medicare certification dates, we find that gaining access to an ostensibly integrated hospital had no effect on Black postneonatal mortality. Similarly, there is little evidence that the campaign contributed to the trend toward in-hospital births among Southern Black mothers. These results are consistent with descriptions of the hospital desegregation campaign as producing only cosmetic changes and illustrate the limits of antidiscrimination policies imposed on reluctant actors.
Journal: The Review of Economics and Statistics

Title: Misperceived Social Norms and Willingness to Act Against Climate Change
Authors: Peter Andre, Teodora Boneva, Felix Chopra, Armin Falk
Affiliations: Leibniz Institute for Financial Research SAFE and Goethe University Frankfurt; University of Bonn; Frankfurt School of Finance and Management
Abstract: Abstract We document the individual willingness to act against climate change and study the role of social norms in a large sample of U.S. adults. Individual beliefs about social norms positively predict pro-climate donations, comparable in strength to universal moral values and economic preferences. However, we document systematic misperceptions of social norms. Respondents vastly underestimate the prevalence of climate-friendly behaviors and norms. Correcting these misperceptions in an experiment causally raises individual willingness to act against climate change and individual support for climate policies. The effects are strongest for individuals who are skeptical about the existence and threat of global warming.
Journal: The Review of Economics and Statistics

Title: The Summer Drop in Female Employment
Authors: Brendan M. Price, Melanie Wasserman
Affiliations: LinkedIn; UCLA and NBER
Abstract: Abstract We provide the first systematic account of summer declines in women’s labor market activity. From May to July, U.S. women’s employment-to-population ratio declines 1.1 p.p., whereas men’s rises; women’s hours worked fall 9.8%, twice the decline among men. School closures for summer break provide a unifying explanation. The summer drop aligns with cross-state differences in school closure timing, is concentrated among mothers with young school-aged children, and coincides with increased time spent on child care. Gender differences both within and across jobs explain gender gaps in summer exits from employment. Women’s summer work interruptions contribute to gender gaps in pay.
Journal: The Review of Economics and Statistics

Title: Coarse Wage Setting and Behavioral Firms
Authors: Germán Reyes
Affiliations: Middlebury College
Abstract: Abstract This paper shows that the bunching of wages at round numbers is partly driven by firm coarse wage setting. Using data from more than 200 million new hires in Brazil, I first establish that contracted salaries tend to cluster at round numbers. Then, I show that firms that tend to hire workers at round-numbered salaries have worse market outcomes. Next, I develop a wage-posting model in which optimization costs lead to the adoption of coarse rounded wages and provide evidence supporting two model predictions using two research designs. Finally, I examine some consequences of coarse wage setting for relevant economic outcomes.
Journal: The Review of Economics and Statistics

Title: Universal Basic Income: Inspecting the Mechanisms
Authors: Nir Jaimovich, Itay Saporta-Eksten, Ofer Setty, Yaniv Yedid-Levi
Affiliations: UCSD, NBER, and CEPR; University of Manchester, Tel Aviv University, CEPR, and IZA; Tel Aviv University; Reichman University (IDC Herzliya)
Abstract: Abstract We examine the mechanisms driving the aggregate and distributional impacts of Universal Basic Income (UBI) through model analysis of various UBI programs and financing schemes. The main adverse effect is the distortionary tax increase to fund UBI, reducing labor force participation. Secondary channels are a decline in demand for self-insurance, depressing aggregate capital, and a positive income effect that further deters labor force participation. Due to these channels, introducing UBI alongside existing social programs reduces output and average welfare. Partially substituting existing programs with UBI mitigates the adverse effects, increases average welfare, but does not deliver a Pareto improvement.
Journal: The Review of Economics and Statistics

Title: Immigration and Worker-Firm Matching
Authors: Gianluca Orefice, Giovanni Peri
Affiliations: University of Paris-Dauphine, PSL, and CESifo; University of California, Davis, and NBER
Abstract: Abstract Positive assortative matching increases both the wages of more productive workers and wage dispersion. We study the effect of immigration on positive assortative matching using French employer-employee data from 1995 to 2005. We find that increases in the share of immigrants, driven by historical networks across local labor markets, generated stronger positive assortative matching between workers and firms. We present evidence suggesting that this effect was associated with higher wages for more productive workers and that the findings are consistent with increased workers’ screening by firms.
Journal: The Review of Economics and Statistics

Title: What Lies Behind the Returns to Schooling: The Role of Labor Market Sorting and Worker Heterogeneity
Authors: Pedro Portugal, Hugo Reis, Paulo Guimarães, Ana Rute Cardoso
Affiliations: Banco de Portugal and NOVA School of Business and Economics, Universidade Nova de Lisboa; Banco de Portugal and Universidade Católica Portuguesa, Católica Lisbon School of Business and Economics; Banco de Portugal and Universidade do Porto, FEP, CEF.UP; IAE-CSIC and Barcelona School of Economics
Abstract: Abstract Do more educated workers earn higher wages partly because they have access to high-paying firms and occupations? We rely on linked employer-employee data to combine the estimation of AKM (Abowd-Kramarz-Margolis) models with the decomposition of the returns to schooling. We exploit exogenous variation in education driven by changes in compulsory education. We show that education provides access to better-paying workplaces and occupations: 30% of the overall return to education operates through the workplace channel and 12% through the occupation channel. The remainder is associated exclusively with the individual. Match quality plays a modest role in the returns to education.
Journal: The Review of Economics and Statistics

Title: Language Barriers in Multinationals and Knowledge Transfers
Authors: Louise Guillouët, Amit K. Khandelwal, Rocco Macchiavello, Madhav Malhotra, Matthieu Teachout
Affiliations: Columbia University; Yale University and NBER; LSE; France Travail
Abstract: Abstract We study communication frictions within multinationals (MNCs), hypothesizing that language barriers reduce management knowledge transfers within the organization. A distinct feature of such MNCs is a three-tier hierarchy: foreign managers (FMs) supervise domestic managers (DMs) who supervise production workers. Tailored surveys from our setting—MNCs in Myanmar—reveal that language barriers impede interactions between FMs and DMs. A first experimental protocol offers DMs free English courses and confirms that lowering communications costs increases their interactions with FMs. A second experimental protocol that asks human-resource managers at domestic firms to rate hypothetical resumes reveals that multinational experience and, specifically, DM-FM interactions are valued in the domestic labor market. Together, these results suggest that reducing language barriers can improve transfers of management knowledge, an interpretation supported by improvements in soft skills among treatment DMs in the first experiment. A model in which communication within MNCs is noncontractible—a realistic feature of workplace life—reveals that the experimental results are consistent with underinvestment in language training and provide a rationale for policy intervention.
Journal: The Review of Economics and Statistics

Title: Time Use and Macroeconomic Uncertainty
Authors: Matteo Cacciatore, Stefano Gnocchi, Daniela Hauser
Affiliations: HEC Montréal, Bank of Canada, and NBER; Bank of Canada
Abstract: Abstract We study the effects of uncertainty on time use and their macroeconomic implications. Employing data from the American Time Use Survey and the Bureau of Labor Statistics, we document that heightened uncertainty increases housework and reduces market hours, mildly impacting leisure. We then propose a model that quantitatively accounts for these estimates. We show that substitution between market and housework provides self-insurance to households, weakening precautionary motives. However, it also reduces aggregate demand, ultimately amplifying uncertainty’s recessionary impact. Time reallocation can lead to higher inflation, particularly when uncertainty is coupled with policies redirecting time use towards housework (e.g., lockdown restrictions).
Journal: The Review of Economics and Statistics

Title: Disentangling the Effects of the 2018–2019 Tariffs on a Globally Connected U.S. Manufacturing Sector
Authors: Aaron Flaaen, Justin Pierce
Affiliations: Federal Reserve Board
Abstract: Abstract This paper estimates the relationship between the U.S. tariff increases of 2018–2019 and outcomes in domestic manufacturing. Despite being intended to boost manufacturing activity, we find U.S. industries more exposed to tariff increases experience relative reductions in employment, as a small positive effect from import protection is offset by larger negative effects from rising input costs and retaliatory tariffs. Higher tariffs are also associated with relative increases in producer prices due to rising input costs. Last, we document broader labor market impacts, as counties more exposed to rising tariffs exhibit relative increases in unemployment and declines in labor force participation.
Journal: The Review of Economics and Statistics

Title: Social Preferences and Redistributive Politics
Authors: Ernst Fehr, Thomas Epper, Julien Senn
Affiliations: University of Zurich; CNRS, IESEG School of Management, Univ. Lille, UMR 9221 - LEM - Lille Economie Management, F-59000 Lille, France and iRisk Research Center on Risk and Uncertainty
Abstract: Abstract We study the link between social preferences and a behaviorally validated measure of support for redistribution. We uncover three fundamentally distinct social preference types: predominantly selfish, inequality averse, and altruistic individuals. Inequality averse and altruistic individuals display a much stronger support for redistribution, particularly if they are more affluent. Beliefs about the role of effort and luck for success play no role for selfish individuals but are highly relevant for other-regarding individuals. Finally, while inequality averse individuals display strong support for policies aimed at reducing the incomes of the rich, altruistic individuals are considerably less supportive of these policies.
Journal: The Review of Economics and Statistics

Title: No Line Left Behind: Assortative Matching Inside the Firm
Authors: Achyuta Adhvaryu, Vittorio Bassi, Anant Nyshadham, Jorge Tamayo
Affiliations: University of California at San Diego; University of Southern California; University of Michigan; Harvard Business School
Abstract: Abstract We leverage the high degree of worker mobility across production lines in a large Indian manufacturer to estimate the sorting of workers to managers, using data on daily worker productivity. We find negative assortative matching (NAM): better workers tend to be matched with worse managers. Estimates of the production technology, however, reveal that productivity would increase by up to 4% under positive sorting. Exploiting a survey of managers and data on orders from multinational brands, we document that NAM arises, at least partly, because maintaining valuable relationships with buyers provides strong incentives to avoid delays on any given production line.
Journal: The Review of Economics and Statistics

Title: A Fundamental Connection: Exchange Rates and Macroeconomic Expectations
Authors: Vania Stavrakeva, Jenny Tang
Affiliations: London Business School; Federal Reserve Bank of Boston
Abstract: Abstract We disprove the exchange rate macroeconomic disconnect puzzle by showing that macroeconomic news can explain most variation in exchange rates at monthly and quarterly frequencies, accounting for up to 91% of the quarterly exchange rate variation during U.S. recessions and 65% over all periods. The main driver of the reconnect is exchange rates responding to past news—a result inconsistent with the theory of uncovered interest rate parity under full information rational expectations (UIP-FIRE). We discuss theoretical models that can explain this surprising result, including models featuring currency risk premia, regulatory or institutional frictions, or deviation from FIRE.
Journal: The Review of Economics and Statistics

Title: The Long-Run Effects of Monetary Policy
Authors: Òscar Jordà, Sanjay R. Singh, Alan M. Taylor
Affiliations: Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco, University of California, Davis and CEPR; Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco and University of California, Davis; Bank of England, Columbia University, NBER, and CEPR
Abstract: Abstract We document that the real effects of monetary shocks last for over a decade. Our approach relies on identification of exogenous and nonsystematic monetary shocks using the trilemma of international finance; merged data from two new international historical cross-country databases; and econometric methods robust to long-horizon inconsistent estimates. Notably, the capital stock and total factor productivity (TFP) exhibit greater hysteresis than labor. When we allow for asymmetry, we find these effects with tightening shocks, but not with loosening shocks. When extending the horizon of the responses reported in several recent studies that use alternative monetary shocks, we find similarly persistent real effects, thus supporting our main findings.
Journal: The Review of Economics and Statistics

Title: Platform capture of scientific knowledge production: publishers’ dominance, generative AI and Subsumption of academic labor
Authors: Ojelanki Ngwenyama, Stefan Klein, Frantz Rowe
Affiliations: Toronto Metropolitan University, Toronto, Canada; University of Cape Town, Cape Town, South Africa; University of Muenster, Muenster; Nantes Universite
Abstract: Academic publishing is dominated by a small group of publishers whose platformization practices are threatening academic institutions and their values. These publishers deploy digital research and publishing platform infrastructures (DRPIs) to capture and transform scientific knowledge production in their private interest. This paper aims at analyzing this shift in the political economy of knowledge production and scholarly communication from expanding use of DRPIs. Using Marx’s theory of subsumption, we empirically analyze the case of Elsevier and its DRPI to theorize platform capture of scientific knowledge production. We find that DRPIs, recently reinforced by generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), enable academic publishers to advance from real subsumption to general intellect subsumption, progressively sidelining academics in scientific knowledge production. Through regimes of marketization, appropriation and exploitation, the leading academic publishers impose structural dominance on academics to appropriate their labor, data and intellectual property rights. Despite the Open Science movement, DRPIs enable the private capture of societal wealth at the expense of epistemic communities and societal good. Without strong collective action, we will not be able to envision DRPIs that fit with academic values, nor will we be able to combat the negative outcomes of advancing platform capture on the institution of science.

Title: Assessing and controlling social desirability bias in self-reported survey research: common practices, recommendations, and an application in cyberbullying research
Authors: Dongyeon Kim, Hyewon Lee, Dong-Heon Kwak, Jose Benitez
Affiliations: Kent State University
Abstract: Social desirability (SD) bias poses a significant challenge in self-reported, survey-based research, leading to the overreporting of socially desirable behaviours and the underreporting of undesirable ones. While previous IS studies have attempted to address SD bias through various strategies—such as prevention, assessment, and control—many have treated it as a procedural formality rather than developing a precise and rigorous approach to managing it effectively. To bridge this gap, this study examines common practices and provides up-to-date recommendations across seven key areas: (1) prevention and assessment, (2) the use of SD scales for detection and control, (3) controlling SD bias in research variables, (4) interpreting SD bias through correlations, (5) its impact on model validity, (6) its effects on causal relationships, and (7) the application of self-deception enhancement and impression management scales for addressing specific biases. Through a comprehensive literature review of prior IS research from these seven perspectives and an empirical examination of the contextual suitability of SD scales in online harassment bystander behaviour, this study offers a more structured and effective approach to detecting and controlling SD bias. By improving the reliability of self-reported data in socially (un)desirable contexts, this research strengthens the validity and methodological rigour of IS findings.

Title: Designing for emergent use recombinations: a conceptual framework for value capture from connectable products
Authors: Gongtai Wang, Susanne Beck, Joe Nandhakumar
Affiliations: Dalian University of Technology; University of Warwick
Abstract: Connectable products, equipped with digital connectivity that allows them to interact with other products, are central to digital innovation. Enabled by the generativity of digital technology, users increasingly engage in emergent use recombinations, generating value beyond firms’ original intentions. This value may not feed back to originating firms through network effects but be appropriated by third parties or remain within local user contexts. Firms relying solely on network effects risk missing new value capture opportunities. We address this challenge by developing a conceptual framework for value capture from connectable products, with particular attention to this aspect. In this broad-theorizing review, we synthesize dispersed insights on value creation and capture in the connectable product literature through the lens of value-path position. Our framework distinguishes three relative positions (touchpoint, bridge, and source) that a connectable product can occupy on a value path, and delineates nine mechanisms through which new value is realized by users, captured by firms, and reinforced by products. This study advances our understanding of capturing value from emergent use recombination, offering firms guidance to proactively recognize, design for, and capture value from emergent use recombinations, while illuminating new directions for research on digital products’ generative potential.

Title: How do attention and emotion drive donations in charitable crowdfunding? An empirical study of users’ cognitive and physiological responses to image content
Authors: Andreas Blicher, Rob Gleasure, Ioanna Constantiou, Jesper Clement
Affiliations: Copenhagen Business School; Department of Marketing, Copenhagen Business School, Copenhagen, Denmark
Abstract: This study investigates the attentional and emotional impact of different image types in medical crowdfunding campaigns, and how these images impact donations. Building on signaling theory and evolutionary explanations for the drivers of altruism, we hypothesized that donors will be more likely to support campaigns with images that depict illness than campaigns with images that do not, and that donors will be more likely to support campaigns with images that depict groups than campaigns with images that depict individuals. We performed an online experiment and a laboratory experiment to test these hypotheses. The results support the hypotheses. Further, consistent with our evolutionary explanations of altruism, we find that images that depict illness receive more immediate attention and arousal than other images, and images that depict multiple individuals receive more total attention than images of individuals. These findings provide valuable insights to help understand how visual information in medical crowdfunding triggers the prioritization of specific fundraisers among potential donors.

Title: Social acceptance of central bank digital currency: insights from the digital euro
Authors: Maximilian Ambros, Michael Frenkel, Christian Schlereth
Affiliations: WHU – Otto Beisheim School of Management, Macroeconomics and International Economics, Vallendar, Germany; WHU – Otto Beisheim School of Management, Digital Marketing, Vallendar, Germany
Abstract: Digital currencies are gaining increasing attention. A current initiative led by the European Central Bank is the introduction of the digital euro, a central bank digital currency (CBDC). As with many large European projects, the success of the digital euro will depend largely on its social acceptance among European citizens. Based on Information Systems theories of technology acceptance and trust, this study examines how social acceptance depends on specific CBDC design choices and to what extent this acceptance varies across major countries in the heterogeneous currency union. To measure social acceptance, we surveyed 1724 respondents and utilised the discrete choice experiment variant SADR (Separated Adaptive Dual Response), which is well-suited if a high degree of heterogeneity in acceptance is possible. Anonymity, merchant acceptance, and monthly fees are the most influential CBDC design attributes. Social acceptance highly depends on the CBDC design choices, which can be as high as 71.6% under favourable conditions, falling to only 21.5% when least favourable conditions are implemented. This paper makes a design-informed, empirically grounded, and policy-relevant contribution by highlighting that CBDC design choices shape social acceptance and that these choices must be evaluated not only for technical soundness but also for their public resonance.

Title: MEDS: Methodology for Evaluation in Design Science
Authors: Richard Baskerville, Jan Pries-Heje, John R. Venable
Affiliations: Georgia State University; Roskilde University; Curtin University
Abstract: Design Science Research (DSR) is a paradigm that centres on the development and evaluation of artefacts. While central, a proper scientific evaluation can significantly increase the work required to complete a DSR project. The high costs, workload, and delays caused by evaluations have been shown to lead to poor or absent evaluations. These findings present two paradoxes: (1) evaluation is considered essential, yet it is commonly done poorly or not at all; (2) DSR promises to improve research relevance through timely artefact development and reliability through scientific evaluation, yet poor and lengthy evaluations cause DSR to often fail to deliver on its promise. To address these paradoxes, this paper presents MEDS (Methods for Evaluation in Design Science), a four-step evaluation method that includes three component methods new to the evaluation guidance literature: MuSCoW (Must, Should, Could, Won’t), the DSR Evaluation Selection Framework, and Short-Scoping of evaluation methods. MEDS aims to address the above paradoxes and guide DSR researchers, especially novices, to achieve a programme of effective and resource-efficient DSR evaluations as an on-going component of existing DSR methodologies. By carefully planning, orchestrating, and scoping evaluation activities, MEDS delivers a rigorous evaluation programme without overwhelming researchers with a massive evaluation burden.

Title: Growing pains: how strategic postures can help and hurt sales growth during periods of severe turbulence
Authors: Ricarda B. Bouncken, Martin Ratzmann
Affiliations: University of Bayreuth
Abstract: Severe turbulence, as evidenced during major crises over the past 15 years, challenges the effectiveness of taken-for-granted strategic stances such as entrepreneurial or digital postures, which are likely to be developed during typical business cycles. Our longitudinal study investigates how firms can protect, or fail to protect, sales growth under the atypical conditions of severe turbulence, depending on their adoption of entrepreneurial and digital postures and their trajectories from pre-turbulence growth. Our findings reveal a paradox: firms with high levels of pre-turbulence growth experience weaker post-turbulence growth when pursuing either a digital posture or an entrepreneurial posture or some combination of both. Instead, firms are most successful in increasing growth when they paradoxically minimise their postures, adopting a “no-posture” stance. Conversely, a no-posture stance proves particularly disadvantageous for firms with low pre-turbulence sales growth leaving these firms in the least favourable position once turbulence subsides. We unpack key mechanisms that explain the paradox.

Title: Security fatigue: manifestation of emotional exhaustion and cynicism by depletion of self-regulation capacity
Authors: Akanksha Malik, Sanjay Goel, Shuchi Sinha
Affiliations: Guildhall School of Business and Law, London Metropolitan University, London, UK; Information Security and Digital Forensics, University at Albany, State University of New York, Albany, New York, USA; Indian Institute of Technology Delhi, New Delhi, India
Abstract: As the cyber threat landscape evolves, organizations are regularly tightening their security policies and procedures, implementing frequent software updates, and update more processes and guidelines, including more stringent password guidelines, and restrictions on data access. These changes trigger stress in employees that over time leads to a depletion of self-regulation capacity and manifests as emotional exhaustion and security associated cynicism in employees which we call security fatigue. This fatigue results in a laxity in compliance with security guidelines and apathy towards security. Using the job demand-resource theory and self-regulation theory, this study conceptualizes security fatigue and attempts to understand the influence of security fatigue on the security compliance behavior of employees. We analyze data from 298 full-time employees, and our results show how organizational (organizational technological support and decision latitude) and personal (self-regulation capacity) resources interact with security demands and work impediments to influence employee security fatigue. Our results also indicate how security fatigue affects the security compliance behavior of employees. The results of the study could provide guidance to organizations in managing security policies and guidelines so as not to exacerbate the security fatigue of employees.

Title: Decomposing Shifts in the Beveridge Curve: Implications for Labor Market Dynamics and Inflation*
Authors: Katharine G. Abraham, John C. Haltiwanger, Lea E. Rendell

Title: WFH and productivity: Evidence from the judiciary
Authors: Andreu Arenas, Marc Bosch, Nerea Frias

Title: Measurement error and peer effects in networks
Authors: Yann Bramoullé, Sebastiaan Maes
Abstract: In many practical applications, only noisy proxies for the true regressors are available, which is commonly believed to induce an attenuation bias. In the linear-in-means model, however, estimated peer effects might be inflated, potentially leading to false positives. This paper shows that the asymptotic bias depends on the interplay between individual characteristics and network links and demonstrates how the network structure can facilitate identification without the need for additional external information. Based on these identification results, we present consistent GMM and 2SLS estimators that are easily implementable. Our results are illustrated by means of a Monte Carlo simulation.

Title: Transaction Costs and the Gains from Trade in Water Markets
Authors: Nick Hagerty
Affiliations: Montana State University nicholas.hagerty@montana.edu
Abstract: Abstract Surface water in California is scarce and tightly managed, yet little is traded through a market. This paper studies transaction costs in the existing wholesale water market and estimates the benefits of reducing them. I develop an empirical framework that uses transactions among water districts to analyze welfare, decomposing prices into demand and transaction costs and simulating a market with only physical frictions. Transaction costs are large: median variable costs are 54% of the price, and fixed costs deter many districts from participating. Eliminating them produces gains of several hundred million dollars per year, or 1-3% of statewide water expenditures.
Journal: The Review of Economics and Statistics

Title: From Micro to Macro in an Equilibrium Diffusion Model
Authors: Wyatt Brooks, Kevin Donovan, Terence R. Johnson
Affiliations: Arizona State University; Yale University and NBER; University of Virginia
Abstract: Abstract We quantify the benefits of better firm-to-firm matching in an aggregate diffusion model where individuals acquire profitable knowledge from others. We estimate the model using a small-scale program in Kenya that creates new opportunities for firm managers to interact. Aggregate gains from the program depend on the relative importance of meeting a high-knowledge firm versus learning within that meeting. We show how moments from the intervention identify these parameters, demonstrating how easily estimated moments beyond the average treatment effect inform at-scale gains. We provide sufficient conditions extending the identification procedure to a broader class of experiments and aggregate diffusion models.
Journal: The Review of Economics and Statistics

Title: Social Ties and Fiscal Transfers in a Regional Economy: A Quantitative Spatial Analysis
Authors: Yuwan Duan, Yatang Lin, Yi Lu
Affiliations: Central University of Finance and Economics; Hong Kong University of Science and Technology; Tsinghua University
Abstract: Abstract Many governments use fiscal transfers to reduce regional inequality, yet discretionary allocation may also depend on informal communication among officials. We examine this mechanism in a large central-to-provincial transfer system, using policymakers’ shared workplace, alumni, and hometown backgrounds to measure social ties. Exploiting ministerial turnover and controlling for provincial leadership, we find that prior workplace ties significantly increase transfers. We then embed these estimates in a quantitative spatial model with trade, migration, input-output linkages, and fiscal-productivity effects. Social ties redirect resources toward richer provinces with stronger fundamentals, raising welfare and output while weakening redistribution. Under egalitarian weights, however, removing ties improves welfare.
Journal: The Review of Economics and Statistics

Title: Insurance Choice with Non-Monetary Plan Attributes: Limited Consideration in Medicare Part D
Authors: Maura Coughlin
Affiliations: Rice University
Abstract: Abstract I propose a model of insurance demand where non-monetary attributes determine which plans an individual considers, and monetary attributes determine an individual's expected utility. This approach reconciles the classic view of insurance as purely financial with the empirical finding that choice is driven by additional attributes. I estimate the model using Medicare Part D data, allowing for unobserved heterogeneity in consideration and preferences. I find the former plays a crucial role: more than 90% of individuals consider 5 or fewer plans, approximately lO°lo of the menu. Additionally, estimates of risk preferences are comparable to existing studies of similar stakes.
Journal: The Review of Economics and Statistics

Title: Scientific Talent Leaks Out of Funding Gaps
Authors: Wei Yang Tham, Joseph Staudt, Elisabeth Ruth Perlman, Stephanie D. Cheng
Affiliations: University of Toronto weiyang.tham@rotman.utoronto.ca; US Census Bureau joseph.staudt@census.gov; US Census Bureau elisabeth.perlman@census.gov; Analysis Group
Abstract: Abstract Federal research funding is a key input into scientific work, but funding streams can be disrupted. We study how delays in renewed NIH research grants affect lab personnel’s careers, linking grant records to university payroll, tax, Census, and publication data. Using a difference-in-differences design, we find that interruptions of at least 30 days increase nonemployment among personnel in labs supported by a single NIH R01 grant by 3 percentage points, or 40%. Among those who remain employed in the US, earnings decrease by 20%. The results show that short funding gaps can alter career trajectories, especially for trainees.
Journal: The Review of Economics and Statistics

Title: Return to Office and the Tenure Distribution
Authors: David Van Dijcke, Florian Gunsilius, Austin Wright
Affiliations: Department of Economics, University of Virginia; Department of Economics, Emory University; Harris School of Public Policy, University of Chicago
Abstract: Abstract Debates over return-to-office mandates have intensified since the COVID-19 pandemic ended, though their economic implications remain poorly understood. Using large-scale resume data, we analyze how these policies affect employee tenure and seniority at three large U.S. tech companies: Microsoft, SpaceX, and Apple. Employing a distributional synthetic controls framework, we estimate a reduction in tenure and seniority at firms returning to the office. We extend the framework with a functional bootstrap procedure and prove its validity for constructing uniform confidence bands. Return-to-office mandates appear to drive senior employees away, posing a risk to firm productivity and innovation.
Journal: The Review of Economics and Statistics

Title: Gender Discrimination in Access to Capital: A Field Experiment in Ethiopia
Authors: Ketki Sheth, Shanthi Manian, Shibiru Ayalew
Affiliations: University of Tennessee, Knoxville ksheth2@utk.edu; Washington State University shanthi@manian.org; Adama Science and Technology University, Ethiopia shibekoo84@gmail.com
Abstract: Abstract We test whether loan officers discriminate against female business owners in capital decisions affecting real businesses in an Ethiopian business plan competition. Randomizing owner gender across 3,696 evaluations, by 84 loan officers, for 916 businesses, we find no effect on prize scores or consideration for a loan. Incentivized beliefs about future performance did not differ by gender, ruling out statistical and taste-based discrimination. Machine learning predictions of future business performance show that loan officers beliefs were accurate. Gender does not meaningfully improve predictions, implying no trade-off between gender equity and effective capital allocation.
Journal: The Review of Economics and Statistics

Title: Job Loss, Unemployment Insurance, and Health: Evidence from Brazil
Authors: Guilherme Amorim, Diogo G. C. Britto, Alexandre Fonseca, Breno Sampaio
Affiliations: University of Georgia amorim@uga.edu; Bocconi University, CLEAN Unit for the Economic Analysis of Crime (INSPIRE/Bocconi), Prospera Lab, CEPR, IZA, IGIER diogo.britto@unibocconi.it; Federal Revenue of Brazil, Prospera Lab, CLEAN Unit for the Economic Analysis of Crime (INSPIRE/Bocconi), GAPPE/UFPE alexandre.fonseca@rfb.gov.br; Federal University of Pernambuco, Prospera Lab, CLEAN Unit for the Economic Analysis of Crime (INSPIRE/Bocconi), GAPPE/UFPE brenorsampaio@gmail.com
Abstract: Abstract We study the health impacts of job loss and unemployment insurance (UI) among Brazilian workers, using unique administrative data linking employment, hospitalizations, health insurance, and mortality records over 17 years. Leveraging mass layoffs for identification, we find that job loss raises hospitalization (+33%) and mortality (+23%) risks for men, with no significant effects for women. Impacts are pervasive across age, income, and education levels, with children of male workers also affected. External causes related to risky behavior and violence victimization explain half the effects. Using a regression discontinuity design, we show that UI partially mitigates health risks, suggesting that these are partially explained by income losses.
Journal: The Review of Economics and Statistics

Title: Estimating the Macroeconomic Effects of Oil Supply News
Authors: Lorenzo Mori, Gert Peersman
Affiliations: Bank of Italy; Ghent University
Abstract: Abstract We show that structural oil-market shocks identified in prominent SVAR models, as well as high-frequency oil price changes around OPEC announcements, are predictable, indicating informational deficiencies in standard oil-market VARs and contamination of commonly used instrumental variables. We resolve these identification problems for oil supply news shocks by augmenting the econometrician’s information set with financial indicators, yielding markedly different results: the shocks induce a sharper short-run output contraction, are less inflationary, contribute less to oil price variation, exhibit greater stability over time, and account for a substantial share of S&P 500 volatility.
Journal: The Review of Economics and Statistics

Title: Gender and Electoral Incentives: Evidence from COVID-19 Response
Authors: Juan Pablo Chauvin, Clemence Tricaud
Affiliations: Inter-American Development Bank juancha@iadb.org; UCLA Anderson and NBER clemence.tricaud@anderson.ucla.edu
Abstract: Abstract This paper provides new evidence on why men and women leaders make different choices. Exploiting Brazilian close elections, we show that female mayors responded differently to the COVID-19 crisis over the year 2020. Female mayors were less likely to close non-essential businesses early in the pandemic and female-led municipalities experienced higher mortality, while the reverse was true later on. We show that these findings can be rationalized by a simple political agency model in which politicians seek re-election and voters are gender biased. Consistent with this interpretation, the gender differences we find are driven exclusively by mayors facing re-election.
Journal: The Review of Economics and Statistics

Title: The Intergenerational Transmission of Employers and the Earnings of Young Workers
Authors: Matthew Staiger
Affiliations: Opportunity Insights and Harvard University mstaiger@g.harvard.edu
Abstract: Abstract This paper investigates how parental connections to firms shape early-career earnings. I use employer-employee linked data to study one important type of connection: jobs obtained at a parent’s employer. Twenty-nine percent of individuals work for a parent’s employer at least once by age 30. Exploiting transitory, firm-specific fluctuations in hiring conditions at the parent’s employer, I estimate that working for a parent’s employer increases initial earnings by 24 percent, primarily by providing access to higher-paying firms. Individuals with higher-earning parents are more likely to work for a parent’s employer and experience larger earnings gains when they do. Consequently, the elasticity of initial earnings with respect to parental earnings would be 12 percent lower if no one found a job through these connections. The findings suggest that connections to firms through one’s social network may be an important determinant of intergenerational mobility.
Journal: The Review of Economics and Statistics

Title: Losing Political Representation
Authors: Timo Wochner, Aaron Günther, Niklas Potrafke, Felix Rösel
Affiliations: ETH Zurich; KOF Institute; CESifo, Munich; University of Munich (LMU); ifo Institute, Munich; TU Braunschweig
Abstract: Abstract What are the consequences of losing political representation in a democracy? A reform of Germany’s mixed electoral system left more than 7 million citizens in 23 constituencies without a directly elected representative after the 2025 national election. Which and how many constituencies were affected was unpredictable and quasi-random. We show that losing geographical representation reduces citizens’ satisfaction with democracy. Moreover, discontent is independent of party preferences and spreads through social networks, reducing democratic satisfaction even among individuals who were unaffected or unaware of the reform’s outcome. We conclude that political representation is a cornerstone of democracy.
Journal: The Review of Economics and Statistics

Title: Intergroup Contact, Empathy Education, and Refugee-Native Integration in Lebanon
Authors: Salma Mousa, Lennard Naumann, Alexandra Scacco
Affiliations: University of California, Los Angeles; WZB Berlin Social Science Center; Humboldt University of Berlin; University of Hamburg
Abstract: Abstract Intergroup contact interventions often yield limited results in deeply divided societies. We test contact and empathy education in Lebanon, where Syrian refugees comprise a quarter of the population. In a fully cross-randomised field experiment with 887 Lebanese and Syrian youth embedded in a psychosocial support programme, we find that contact has little effect on outgroup attitudes and behaviour, while empathy education consistently improves attitudes for Lebanese youth and behavioural engagement for both. The combined treatment achieves little beyond empathy alone, with no evidence of spillovers to parents (n = 595). In polarised settings, empathy education should precede — or replace — contact.

Title: Feeling rich or looking rich? Self-perceived vs socially-perceived relative income
Authors: Nicolas Bottan, Ricardo Perez-Truglia, Hitoshi Shigeoka, Katsunori Yamada

Title: Joint capacity planning and dynamic allocation for container leasing with asymmetric substitution
Authors: Kang Chen, Zhikang Wang, Mingzhu Zong, Zhongzhen Yang, Jihong Chen, Xu Xin

Title: Scaling data management capabilities for enterprise AI: a maturity model for the banking industry
Authors: Nico Baum, Lea Mueller-Fortmann, Alexander Benlian
Affiliations: Technical University of Darmstadt – TU Darmstadt
Abstract: Integrating artificial intelligence (AI) into financial institutions requires more than deploying technical solutions. It requires data management capabilities (DMCs) aligned with regulatory constraints and strategic priorities. This clinical study investigates how a German bank evolved from fragmented, Excel-based processes to a cloud-enabled data environment supporting AI enablement. Using a longitudinal embedded clinical case study, we trace the development of DMCs across three transformation phases and show how executives institutionalized interdependent DMCs through iterative cycles of experimentation, negotiation, and learning. We identify five mutually reinforcing capability domains: (1) Technology and Infrastructure, (2) Data Governance and Quality, (3) Cultural and Organizational Shifts, (4) Regulatory Compliance and Risk Management, and (5) AI Enablement. We contribute to IS research by (1) developing a grounded DMC maturity model that translates these insights into a practical diagnostic tool, (2) providing a process-based lens on cumulative DMC development that highlights sociocultural readiness and recurring managerial missteps as central mechanisms, explaining how readiness builds toward scaled AI enablement in regulated environments, and (3) extending clinical IS research by demonstrating how embedded inquiry can generate context-aware artifacts to support AI transformation. For practitioners, the maturity model provides diagnostic signals, minimum viable actions, and readiness evidence for scaling trustworthy AI.

Title: Media Slant is Contagious
Authors: Philine Widmer, Clémentine Abed Meraim, Sergio Galletta, Elliott Ash
Affiliations: Paris School of Economics; Princeton University; ETH Zürich
Abstract: Abstract This paper examines the diffusion of media slant. We document the influence of Fox News Channel (FNC) on the partisan slant of local newspapers in the U.S. over the years 1995-2008. We measure the political slant of local newspapers by scaling the news article texts to Republicans’ and Democrats’ speeches in Congress. Using channel positioning as an instrument for viewership, we find that higher FNC viewership causes local newspapers to adopt more right-wing slant. The effect emerges gradually, only several years after FNC’s introduction, mirroring the channel’s growing influence on voting behaviour. A main driver of the shift in newspaper slant appears to be a change in local political preferences.

Title: Top income taxation: Efficiency, social welfare and the Laffer curve
Authors: Jacob Lundberg
Abstract: This paper develops a structural framework for analyzing top income taxation and applies it to six decades of U.S. tax history and to eight other advanced economies. The paper derives explicit expressions for top-bracket tax revenue and total excess burden across the full range of tax rates, while preserving local consistency with the sufficient-statistics approach of Saez (2001) . Applied to the United States, the analysis implies that the current excess burden of the top federal tax bracket is $101 billion and that raising the top marginal tax rate to its revenue-maximizing level of 72 percent would increase annual revenue by $111 billion, given a taxable income elasticity of 0.25. The current tax rate is lower than what is consistent with a purely utility-based notion of social welfare. By contrast, Nordic countries and the United States in earlier decades appear to have operated at tax rates exceeding revenue-maximizing levels.

Title: Prosecutor politics: The impact of election cycles on criminal sentencing in the era of rising incarceration
Authors: Chika O. Okafor
Abstract: I investigate how political incentives affect the behavior of district attorneys (DAs). I develop a theoretical model that predicts DAs will increase sentencing intensity in an election period compared to the period prior. To empirically test this prediction, I compile one of the most comprehensive datasets to date on the political careers of all district attorneys in office during the steepest rise in incarceration in U.S. history (roughly 1986-2006). Using quasi-experimental methods, I find causal evidence that being in a DA election year increases total admissions per capita and total months sentenced per capita. I estimate that the election year effects on admissions are akin to moving 0.85 standard deviations along the distribution of DA behavior within state (e.g., going from the 50th to 80th percentile in sentencing intensity). I find evidence that election effects are larger (1) when DA elections are contested, (2) in Republican counties, and (3) in the southern United States--all these factors are consistent with the perspective that election effects arise from political incentives influencing DAs. Further, I find that district attorney election effects decline over the period 1986-2006, in tandem with U.S. public opinion softening regarding criminal punishment. These findings suggest DA behavior may respond to voter preferences--in particular to public sentiment regarding the harshness of the court system.

Title: When stability becomes a liability: the negative effects of supplier network stability on green innovation diversity and quality
Authors: Qiuxia Zheng, Shan Liu, Jing Tan
Affiliations: School of Management, Xi'an Jiaotong University; ESADE Business School, Universitat Ramon Llull
Abstract: Purpose Drawing on the network embeddedness perspective, this study aims to investigate how supplier network stability affects two distinct facets of green innovation – diversity and quality – and how these relationships are moderated by absorptive capacity. Design/methodology/approach The proposed relationships are tested using ordinary least squares regression based on a sample of 1,655 firm-year observations from 577 Chinese publicly listed firms over the period 2009–2023. To address potential endogeneity and selection bias, we conduct a series of analyses. Findings We find that supplier network stability is detrimental to both green innovation diversity and green innovation quality. Furthermore, absorptive capacity plays a differential moderating role, alleviating the detrimental influence of supplier network stability on green innovation quality while having no significant moderating effect on green innovation diversity. Originality/value By integrating the network embeddedness perspective with the green innovation literature, this study uncovers the unintended consequences of supplier network stability for green innovation diversity and quality and underscores the important role of absorptive capacity in mitigating these adverse effects.
Journal: International Journal of Operations & Production Management

Title: A Quantile Model of Firm Investment
Authors: Heitor Almeida, Murillo Campello, Luciano de Castro, Antonio F. Galvao
Affiliations: Department of Finance University of Illinois and NBER, Champaign, illinois, USA; Department of Finance University of Florida and NBER Gainesville Florida USA; Department of Economics University of Iowa Iowa City Iowa USA; Department of Economics Michigan State University East Lansing Michigan USA
Abstract: ABSTRACT Are firms risk averse? We propose a dynamic model of firm investment under uncertainty that captures firms' risk attitudes through quantile preferences. The firm maximizes its present value, defined as current profits and investment plus the discounted value of the ‐quantile of its value next period. The model implies that the firm's investment policy equates the marginal cost of capital with the ‐quantile of the discounted present value of future marginal profits. Therefore, investment depends directly on the firm's risk attitude. Empirical estimations using the Euler equation derived from the quantile investment model reveal evidence of downside risk aversion.

Title: Discussion of “Human Capital as a Driver of Automation: Theory and Evidence from China's College Expansion”
Authors: Zhang Chen
